$$
\Delta V = -\beta \cdot V \cdot \Delta P
$$

Where:
- $\Delta V$ is the change in volume,
- $\beta = 20 \times 10^{-6} \, \text{per atm}$ is the compressibility of the oil,
- $V = 5 \, \text{ft}^3$ is the initial volume,
- $\Delta P$ is the applied pressure in atmospheres (atm).

$$
\Delta P = \frac{2000}{14.7} \approx 136.05 \, \text{atm}
$$

---

$$
\Delta V = - (20 \times 10^{-6}) \cdot 5 \cdot 136.05
$$

$$
\Delta V = - (20 \times 10^{-6}) \cdot 680.25 = -0.013605 \, \text{ft}^3
$$

$$
\Delta V \approx -0.0136 \, \text{ft}^3
$$

To determine the boiling point of water at the top of Mount Everest (where the pressure is 253 Torr), we use the Clausius-Clapeyron equation, which relates vapor pressure to temperature:

$$
\ln\left(\frac{P_2}{P_1}\right) = \frac{\Delta H_{\text{vap}}}{R} \left( \frac{1}{T_1} - \frac{1}{T_2} \right)
$$

### Given:
- $\Delta H_{\text{vaporization}} = 40.656\ \mathrm{kJ/mol} = 40656\ \mathrm{J/mol}$
- $T_1 = 373.12\ \mathrm{K}$ (normal boiling point of water)
- $P_1 = 760\ \mathrm{Torr}$ (standard atmospheric pressure)
- $P_2 = 253\ \mathrm{Torr}$ (pressure at the top of Mount Everest)
- $R = 8.314\ \mathrm{J/mol \cdot K}$

---

### Step 1: Compute the natural log of the pressure ratio

$$
\ln\left(\frac{253}{760}\right) = \ln(0.3329) \approx -1.1
$$

---

### Step 2: Plug values into the Clausius-Clapeyron equation

$$
-1.1 = \frac{40656}{8.314} \left( \frac{1}{373.12} - \frac{1}{T_2} \right)
$$

$$
\frac{40656}{8.314} \approx 4890\ \mathrm{K}
$$

$$
-1.1 = 4890 \left( \frac{1}{373.12} - \frac{1}{T_2} \right)
$$

$$
\frac{1}{373.12} \approx 0.002681\ \mathrm{K^{-1}}
$$

$$
-1.1 = 4890 \left( 0.002681 - \frac{1}{T_2} \right)
$$

$$
0.002681 - \frac{1}{T_2} = \frac{-1.1}{4890} \approx -0.000225
$$

$$
\frac{1}{T_2} = 0.002681 + 0.000225 = 0.002906\ \mathrm{K^{-1}}
$$

$$
T_2 = \frac{1}{0.002906} \approx 344\ \mathrm{K}
$$

---

### Final Answer:

$$
\text{The boiling point of water at the top of Mount Everest is approximately } \boxed{344}\ \mathrm{K}.
$$
